notes.text: That they should gather a double portion on the sixth day, ver. 22-26.
That they should expect none on the seventh day, ver. 27-31,

That they should preserve a pot of it for a memorial, ver 32.

1. A month's provision, it seems, the host of Israel took with them out of Egypt, when they came thence on the 15th day of the first month, which, by the 15th day of the second month, was all spent.

2. Then the whole congregation murmured against Moses and Aaron - God's viceregents among them.

3. They so undervalue their deliverance, that they wish, they had died in Egypt, nay, and died by the hand of the Lord too. That is, by some of the plagues which cut off the Egyptians; as if it were not the hand of the Lord, but of Moses only, that brought them into this wilderness. 'Tis common for people to say of that pain, or sickness, which they see not second causes of, It is what pleaseth God, as if that were not so likewise which comes by the hand of man, or some visible accident. We cannot suppose they had any great plenty in Egypt, how largely soever they now talk of the flesh-pots, nor could they fear dying for want in the wilderness while they had their flocks and herds with them; but discontent magnifies what is past, and vilifies what is present, without regard to truth or reason. None talk more absurdly than murmurers.

4. Man being made out of the earth, his Maker has wisely ordered him food out of the earth, Psalm civ, 14. But the people of Israel typifying the church of the first-born that are written in heaven, receiving their charters, laws and commissions from heaven, from heaven also they received their food. See what God designed in making this provision for them, that I may prove them whether they will walk in my law or no - Whether they will trust me, and whether they would serve him, and be ever faithful to so good a master.
They shall prepare — Lay up, grind, bake or boil.
The Lord — And not we, (as you suggest) by our own counsel.
The glory of the Lord — An extra-ordinary and sudden brightness.

And ye shall know that I am the Lord your God — This gave proof of his power as the Lord, and his particular favour to them as their God; when God plagued the Egyptians, it was to make them know that he is the Lord; when he provided for the Israelites, it was to make them know that he was their God.

The quails came up, and covered the camp — So tame that they might take up as many of them as they pleased. Next morning he rained manna upon them, which was to be continued to them for their daily bread.

What is this? Manna descended from the clouds. It came down in dew melted, and yet was itself of such a consistency as to serve for nourishing strengthening food, without any thing else: It was pleasant food; the Jews say it was palatable to all, according as their tastes were. It was wholesome food, light of digestion. By this spare and plain diet we are all taught a lesson of temperance, and forbidden to desire dainties and varieties.

glossa.text:
*And all the congregation of Israel murmured,* etc. ((ORIG., homil. 7 in Exod.)) O ungrateful people! it desires Egypt, it that saw the Egyptians destroyed; and the flesh of Egypt, it that sees the flesh of the Egyptians given both to the fishes and to the birds! It murmurs against Moses, nay rather against God; but the first time pardon is granted, and the second, and perhaps the third: but if they do not cease, but persist, hear what follows, it is related in the book of Numbers ((Num. XXI)), and the same Apostle rehearses it, saying ((I Cor. X)): *Neither do you murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the serpents. These things were written on account of us, upon whom the ends of the world are come.* But if we do not cease to murmur and complain against God, we shall incur a like peril of offence, or a like example of it. For when we lay the blame upon the inclemency of the heavens, the unfruitfulness of the crops, the rarity of showers, and upon the prosperity of some and the unprosperity of others, we murmur against God. But these things are pardoned at first, and are severely avenged upon those who persist, because serpents shall be sent upon them, that is, they shall be handed over to unclean and poisonous spirits, which by hidden bites feed upon the inner chambers of the heart.

((ORIG.)) For the correction of those who read, the sin of the people is set down: that it murmured and was ungrateful for the divine benefits, when it had received the heavenly manna. In the second month, on the fifteenth day of the month, which is not written without reason. Recall the laws of the pasch which were spoken ((Num. IX)), and thou wilt find there that this is the time which is appointed for the keeping of a second pasch by those who have been unclean in soul, or taken up with business abroad. Those who had not been unclean in soul, or were not journeying far off, kept the pasch on the fourteenth day of the first month; but those far off on pilgrimage, and the unclean, keep the second pasch at this time, in which the manna came down from heaven. On the day on which the first pasch is kept, the manna does not come down, but on that on which the second is kept: the first pasch is that of the Jewish people; the second is ours. For we were unclean in soul, we who *worshipped idols; and we were pilgrims, and far off, strangers and pilgrims from the testaments of God,* etc. ((Eph. II.)) But manna is given from heaven, not on the day on which the first pasch is kept, but on that on which the second is: *For the bread which came down from heaven ((Joan. VI))* did not come to those who were celebrating the first solemnity, but to us, who have received the second. *For Christ our pasch is sacrificed, who as true man came down as bread from heaven ((I Cor. V.))* Let us see meanwhile what is shown to have been done on this day: On the fourteenth day of the second month the people murmured, etc.
*We sat over the fleshpots,* etc. They had flocks of sheep and herds of oxen, of which they could eat; but they burned with desire for the fish and the fowl in which Egypt abounds.

*Behold I will rain,* etc. ((ORIG., homil. 8 in Exod.)) I should wish first to have a discourse upon this scripture with the Jews, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted, as to what seems to them of that which it says: *For six days together you shall gather, but on the sixth day double.* It appears therefore that that day is named the sixth which is set before the sabbath; but the sabbath is the seventh day. I ask therefore on what day the manna began to be given? and I wish to compare our Lord's day with the sabbath of the Jews. For from Scripture it appears that on the Lord's day the manna is first given, gathered for six days together; on the seventh, which is the sabbath, there is a ceasing. Since therefore on the Lord's day God rained manna, and not on the sabbath, let the Jews understand that even then our Lord's day was preferred to their sabbath; and it was signified that on that day the grace of God did not come down from heaven to them, and that the heavenly bread, which is the word of God, did not reach them; whence Osee III: *For many days the children of Israel shall sit without king, without prince, without victim, without sacrifice, without priest.* But on our Lord's day the Lord always rains manna, that is, the heavenly words which are joyful to us. Those unhappy men sigh even after manna as their fathers did, and do not deserve to receive it; for they cannot eat what is small like coriander seed, and white like hoar frost. For they perceive nothing in the word of God that is small, subtle and spiritual, but all of it fat and gross. *For the heart of this people is grown gross.* The interpretation also of this name sounds thus. For manna is interpreted *What is this?* The very force of the name invites to learning, so that when thou hearest the law of God recited, thou mayest always inquire and say to the teachers, *What is this?* Thou therefore, if thou wilt eat manna, and receive the word of God, know that it is small and very subtle, like coriander seed: for it has somewhat of the herb whereby it can nourish and refresh the weak. *For he that is weak eateth herbs ((Rom. XIV))*. For it has also somewhat of sharpness, and therefore is as hoar frost; but of whiteness and sweetness very much. What is whiter, more splendid, than divine learning? what sweeter, more delightful, than the words of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb?

*Loaves.* The manna, namely: it is a manner of speech by which bread is put for food; and Scripture loves rather to say *loaves* in the plural than *bread* in the singular.

*That I may prove.* This proving is a testing, not a seducing to sin; nor are they proved for this reason, that God did not know: but he shows them to themselves, that they may become the more humble in asking help and in acknowledging the grace of God.

*But on the sixth day,* etc. ((ORIG., hom. 7.)) On the sixth day let double be gathered into store, as much as may suffice also for the sabbath. The sixth day is this life in which we now are, whence in six days God made this world; on this day therefore we ought to lay up as much as will suffice in the world to come. For if thou acquire here anything of good work, if thou lay up to thy credit anything of justice, of mercy and of piety, this will be food for thee in the world to come. For he who acquires here ten talents ((Luc. XIX)), there shall receive ten cities, and *what a man shall sow, that also shall he reap ((Gal. VI))*. The rich of this world lay up those things which are corrupted in this world, nay together with this world: but goods laid up remain until the morrow. And it is written. *They who were unfaithful kept of the manna, and worms boiled forth out of it and it putrefied;* but what was laid up for the day of the sabbath remained whole. And thou therefore, if for the sake of the present life and the love of the world thou lay up treasure, straightway worms boil forth, of which it is said in Isaias LXVI: *Their worm dieth not;* these are begotten by avarice and the blind greed of riches in those who have money, and who, seeing their brethren in need, shut up their bowels from them. Whence the Apostle ((I Tim. VI)) charges *the rich not to be highminded, nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches,* etc.; nor do worms come to be in us from any other source than from the manna, that is, the word of God. Whence John XV: *If I had not come and spoken to them,* etc. After the word of God has been received, therefore, if anyone sins, that very word is made a worm, which ever digs into his conscience and gnaws the secret places of his breast.

((ORIG.)) *In the evening you shall know,* etc. *Toward evening you shall know that I am the Lord; and in the morning you shall see the majesty of the Lord.* Let the Jews answer me how the Lord is known toward evening, and his majesty seen in the morning? Where was he acknowledged toward evening, and his majesty seen in the morning? But this is not understood save in the Gospel ((Matth. XXVIII)), in which on the evening of the sabbath, which *dawneth on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalen came and the other Mary to the sepulchre, and they found the stone rolled back from the monument, and an earthquake made,* and the monuments opened, and the centurion and the guards of the sepulchre saying: *Indeed this was the Son of God.* The Lord was acknowledged in this evening, because he himself was the Lord: he was acknowledged in the power of the resurrection, and in the morning his glory was seen. When the other women had come on the first day of the week very early in the morning, they found angels sitting at the sepulchre with great brightness, and saying: *He is not here, but is risen from the dead. Come and see the place,* etc. ((Luc. XXIV.)) His majesty therefore was seen in the morning, because the resurrection also was announced by angels.

*But what are we,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 59 in Exod., tom. III.)) They wished that they availed not so much as God, etc., *as far as* he showed the Holy Spirit to be God by adding, Acts V: *Thou hast not lied to men, but to God.*

*In the evening you shall eat flesh* ((ORIG., ut supra. )) Morally we can understand that for each one of us there is a morning and a beginning of the day, the time in which we are first enlightened and kindled to the light of faith. In this time we cannot eat the flesh of the word, that is, we are not yet capable of perfect doctrine; but after long exercises, after very much progress, when we are already near to evening, that is, to the faith of perfection, then we are made capable of more solid food. Let us hasten therefore to receive the manna, which yields in the mouth what savour each one wills. Whence Matthew IX: *Be it done to thee according to thy faith.* And thou therefore, if thou receive with all faith and devotion the word of God which is preached in the Church, be it done to thee whatsoever thou desirest. If thou art in tribulation, it consoles thee, saying: *A contrite and humbled heart God spurneth not ((Psal. L))* ; if thou rejoicest for the hope to come, it heaps up joys for thee, saying: *Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye just ((Psal. XXXI))*; if thou art wrathful, it says: *Cease from anger, and leave indignation ((Psal. XXXVI))* ; if thou art in griefs, it heals thee, saying: *The Lord healeth all thy diseases ((Matth. IV))*; if thou art consumed by poverty, it says in consolation: *The Lord lifteth the needy from the earth, and raiseth up the poor out of the dunghill ((Psal. CXII))* . Yet if anyone receives it unfaithfully, and does not eat it, but hides it, worms boil forth out of it. Nor be thou troubled if the word of God is brought to this, that it is thought to be made a worm; for he himself says: *I am a worm, and no man ((Psal. XXI))*. For as he himself is the one who becomes to some a ruin, but to others a resurrection ((Luc. II)); so also is he the one who in the manna is made to the faithful the sweetness of honey, to the unfaithful a worm. For he is the word of God which convicts the minds of the wicked and pierces the conscience with the darts of correction. For he is the one who is made fire to those to whom he opens the Scriptures , who say: *Was not our heart burning within us?* etc. ((Luc. XXIV.)) To others he is fire, in whom he burns up the thorns of the evil earth, that is, consumes evil thoughts in the heart; and therefore for sinners neither does the convicting worm ever die, nor is the burning fire quenched: but for the just and the faithful he remains sweet and pleasant. Whence it is said in psalm XXXIII: *Taste and see,* etc.


[n: (ORIG., ubi supra. )] Another reading: *In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with loaves.* Let the Jews say what consequence there is, that in the evening they should eat flesh without loaves, or in the morning loaves without meat? what of the divine gift, what of the tempering of heavenly grace, is shown in this? Is this that wherein they can acknowledge God, who eat flesh in the evening without loaves, [0238C] and do they say that the majesty of God appears, if again loaves are eaten without flesh? let them keep such things to themselves, for those who, acquiescing in you, think that God is acknowledged in quails; but we, for whom at the end, toward the evening of the world, the Word was made flesh, say that God is acknowledged in that flesh only which he took from the Virgin: for this flesh of the Word of God no one ate either in the morning or at noon, but toward evening: for the coming of the Lord in the flesh was made toward evening, as John also says: *Children, it is the last hour [n: (I Joan. II)]* [var: Vulg. 1Jo 2:18 has *Filioli*, "Little children"] .-- *In the morning,* he says, *you shall be filled with loaves.* To us therefore the bread is the Word of God: *He is the living bread which came down from heaven, and giveth life to the world [n: (Joan. VI)]*. But as to its saying that this bread is given in the morning, whereas he was incarnate toward evening, it is so to be understood [0238D] that the Lord came toward the evening of the world and near its end; but by his coming, since he is the sun of justice, he restored a new morning to believers; a new light, namely, of knowledge, in which they are filled with loaves who have received his precepts. Nor wonder that the word is called both the flesh of God, and bread, and is called milk and herbs, and is named diversely according to the measure of believers and the capacity of those who take it. Or, after the morning made by the resurrection, he filled believers with loaves, because he granted the books of the law and the prophets, before unknown, for the instruction of the Church, and he himself is made bread in the Gospel, while the other books of the law and the prophets or of the histories may be called many loaves, with which believers from among the Gentiles are filled. Whence: *They shall go up into the mountain, and [0239A] shall drink wine, they shall be anointed with ointment.* Fittingly therefore do we receive flesh toward evening and are filled with loaves in the morning: because neither could we eat flesh in the morning, for the time was not yet; nor at noon, for scarcely do the angels eat flesh at noon, and to that order perhaps the noonday time is granted.

*And in the morning.* On the ninth day, when Christ, the sun of justice, by his coming restored to believers the things that were lost.

[n: (ISID.)] By the food of birds is figured the preaching divinely sent, which runs through sounding words, as winged things through the air, on which they are fed by faith who set out for the heavenly fatherland. Or the utterances of the old law, which fed the carnal people as with flesh through words divinely sent, as through flying things. Whence also it is given in the evening, because [0239B] all things granted to them carnally were to have an end. But in the manifest light of faith the manna is given, which is Christ, namely the *living bread which came down from heaven [n: (Joan. VI)]*, who is rained through the evangelical clouds upon the whole world: not now upon the murmuring and tempted Synagogue, but upon the believing and hoping Church.

*In the likeness of hoar frost upon the earth.* The hoar frost signifies Christ: for the manna was first given on the Lord's day, and Christ rose again on the Lord's day.

*Pounded.* That is, most clean. For as wheat, or millet, or some other such thing is bruised in a little mortar with a pestle and stripped of its husks, so the body of Christ was stripped of mortality through the tribulation of the passion and the pestle of the cross. Or the small manna is the subtlety of heavenly doctrine, which is pounded with the pestle that the literal sense may be stripped away.

*Man hu. ((GREG., lib. XXVII Moral., cap. 7.))* What is designated by the manna given from above to the children of Israel, save the wonder of the heavenly sweetness? For sweet is the food which is received from on high; it is called *man hu*, which is interpreted *What is this?* which we say when we behold what we wonder at not knowing. The soul therefore perceives the heavenly manna, when, lifted up by the voice of compunction, it is astonished at the new appearance of the eternal refreshment, so that, filled with the divine sweetness, it may rightly answer *What is this?* because while it is held suspended away from the lowest thought, it beholds those things which are from on high and wonders at them as at things unwonted. And when by this voice the deafness of our torpor is broken, the practice of the old life is changed, so that the soul, breathed upon by the heavenly Spirit, both desires in the highest things what it had despised, and despises in the lowest things what it had desired.

notes.text: Glory — Glory in the God whom you serve, as the only true God.
Seek — The Lord in his strength, in his sanctuary, or before the ark, which is called God's strength. Face - His gracious presence.
Judgments — The punishments which he brought upon Egypt by his mere word.
Of Jacob — The only branch of Abraham's seed to whom the following blessings belong.

glossa.text:
*Alleluia.* ((CASS.)) Here for the first time *alleluia,* nor was it set down before this by anyone; and no tongue has presumed to change it. *Alleluia,* praise ye. *Ia* is the name of the invisible God, which belongs to him alone. Through twenty psalms, which have this title, the great works of God are told, and great is the exultation in them. ((CASS.)) Here the prophet commends the good among that people of Israel, who together with other believers are the true seed of Abraham, the children of the promise.

*Give glory to the Lord.* ((AUG.)) The first psalm to which alleluia is prefixed, etc., *as far as* he subjoins what temporal things the mercy of God gave them.
*All things:* ((CASS.)) all things; there is nothing that shame should keep silent. Or, all the things which they shall tell are wonderful, for no one can relate them all.

*Be ye praised in the name,* that is, rejoice that you are called Christians from Christ.

((AUG.)) Be ye praised: he does not forbid being praised, if they are good; if they are not, then not save in the Lord, who makes men good. Be ye praised in the name. Which elsewhere is, *In the Lord shall my soul be praised:* what he adds there, *let the meek hear and rejoice:* here too in a manner, *let the heart rejoice,* as if he should say,

*The face,* etc. ((ID.)) That is, the presence, etc., *as far as* the wicked man can fear the presence which the good man loves. ((HIER.)) From the martyr Hippolytus, etc., *as far as* there about to take his Church from among the Gentiles.

*Remember, and the rest.* ((AUG.)) Seek him, etc., *as far as* if it is a great thing to seek what God is, at least behold the things which he has made. *The wonders,* etc. ((ID.)) Little by little he ascends from visible wonders to judgments: thence to the everlasting testament, where there is both precept and promise.

notes.text: To me to live is Christ — To know, to love, to follow Christ, is my life, my glory, my joy.

Here he begins to treat of the former clause of the preceding verse. Of the latter he treats, chap. ii, 17. But if I am to live is the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour — This is the fruit of my living longer, that I can labour more. Glorious labour! desirable fruit! in this view, long life is indeed a blessing. And what I should choose I know not - That is, if it were left to my choice.
To depart — Out of bonds, flesh, the world. And to be with Christ - In a nearer and fuller union. It is better to depart; it is far better to be with Christ.
I know — By a prophetic notice given him while he was writing this. That I shall continue some time longer with you - And doubtless he did see them after this confinement.

Only — Be careful for this, and nothing else. Stand fast in one spirit - With the most perfect unanimity. Striving together - With united strength and endeavours. For the faith of the gospel - For all the blessings revealed and promised therein.
Which — Namely, their being adversaries to the word of God, and to you the messengers of God. Is an evident token - That they are in the high road to perdition; and you, in the way of salvation.
For to you it is given — As a special token of God's love, and of your being in the way of salvation.
Having the same kind of conflict with your adversaries, which ye saw in me — When I was with you, Acts xvi, 12, 19, &c.

glossa.text: *But to me to live is Christ,* etc. As if he would say: Deservedly do I magnify Christ, whether by life or by death, because *Christ is to me to live,* that is, he is life to me here through faith and hope, and in the future through sight. For this life he delivered up his mortal body, that he may receive that same body immortal for ever, whence he also subjoins, and to die is gain.

*But if to live,* etc. Christ is to me to live, that I may magnify him. And if that is so, then I know not which I should choose, to die or to live. As if: Unless this fruit were, there would be no doubt but that I would choose to die, that I might have Christ for my reward: and therefore, do not doubt to die for Christ.
*But to abide,* etc. Behold, he chooses not what is better for himself, but what is expedient for many, on account of charity, which is to be chosen before all things.
*And the joy of faith,* etc. That is: That we may rejoice over your faith, or that you may rejoice over the faith, advancing in it. Which is not save where there is a clean conscience.
*And this from God,* etc. Even that which you suffer is not from you, but from God: because, for the merit of Christ who obeyed the Father, this among the other graces has been given to you.
*Not only,* etc. Both therefore pertain to the grace of God, both the faith of them that believe and the endurance of them that suffer, because he said that both were given.
*Such as you have both seen in me.* When I was scourged naked on account of the pythoness woman out of whom I shut out the malignant spirit, who furnished great gain to her masters.

notes.text: That some of those who were first called may yet be last, our Lord confirms by the following parable: of which the primary scope is, to show, That many of the Jews would be rejected, and many of the Gentiles accepted; the secondary, That of the Gentiles, many who were first converted would be last and lowest in the kingdom of glory; and many of those who were last converted would be first, and highest therein. The kingdom of heaven is like — That is, the manner of God's proceeding in his kingdom resembles that of a householder. In the morning - At six, called by the Roman and Jews, the first hour. From thence reckoning on to the evening, they called nine, the third hour; twelve, the sixth; three in the afternoon, the ninth; and five, the eleventh. To hire labourers into his vineyard - All who profess to be Christians are in this sense labourers, and are supposed during their life to be working in God's vineyard.
The Roman penny was about seven pence halfpenny. [About thirteen and three quarter cents, American.] This was then the usual price of a day's labour.
About the eleventh hour — That is, very late; long after the rest were called.
In the evening — Of life; or of the world.

Who were hired about the eleventh hour — Either the Gentiles, who were called long after the Jews into the vineyard of the Church of Christ; or those in every age who did not hear, or at least understand the Gospel call, till their day of life was drawing to a period. Some circumstances of the parable seem best to suit the former, some the latter of these senses.
The first supposed they should have received more — Probably the first here may mean the Jews, who supposed they should always be preferred before the Gentiles.

Thou hast made them equal to us — So St. Peter expressly, Acts xv, 9. God-hath put no difference between us (Jews) and them, (Gentiles, ) purifying their hearts by faith. And those who were equally holy here, whenever they were called, will be equally happy hereafter.

It is my will to give to this last called among the heathens even as to the first called among the Jews: yea, and to the late converted publicans and sinners, even as to those who, were called long before.

Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? — Yea, doubtless, to give either to Jew or Gentile a reward infinitely greater than he deserves. But can it be inferred from hence, that it is lawful, or possible, for the merciful Father of spirits to "Consign an unborn soul to hell? Or damn him from his mother's womb?" Is thine eye evil because I am good - Art thou envious, because I am gracious? Here is an evident reference to that malignant aspect, which is generally the attendant of a selfish and envious temper.

So the last shall be first, and the first last — Not only with regard to the Jews and Gentiles, but in a thousand other instances. For many are called - All who hear the Gospel; but few chosen - Only those who obey it. Matt. xix, 30; xxii, 14.

glossa.text: *The kingdom is like.* He shows by a parable that the first shall be last, and the last first. This father of the household is our Creator, who has a vineyard, the universal Church, which from Abel to the last of the elect who is to be born at the end has sent forth as many branches as it has brought forth saints. This father went out to dress his vineyard in the morning, at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, the eleventh he hired workmen, from the beginning of this world to its end: he does not cease to send preachers to school the people of the faithful. *The kingdom is like.* Not to the man only, but to the whole business carried on by the man, and so likewise in like cases. *Early in the morning.* Plainly he began from the first just man to invite preachers, with an everlasting wage, to plant the Church.

*By agreement.* That is, by a confirmed promise that they should be reformed to the image of God, if by building up the Church they should press on in the commandments of the decalogue.

*For a penny. ((HIER.))* The penny bears the image of the king, etc., *as far as* or in your last days come to your senses.

*From the last even unto,* etc. Because those who at the Lord's coming have been called to the kingdom arrive without any lateness, equal to those who began from the beginning of the world, all indeed have the same heaven, but star differs from star in brightness. He began from the last, when he brought the thief into paradise before Peter. Because those who come late are sometimes rewarded first, because they go forth out of the body before those who were called in boyhood.

*Or is it not lawful.* A foolish question against the goodness of God. The thing to be asked would be, not whether he gave what he did not owe: but whether he did not give what he did owe. *Is thy eye,* etc. Truly the Jews had a crooked intent, who forbade the apostles to speak to the Gentiles, that they might be saved.

*So the last shall be first. ((AUG.))* That is, the Jews shall be turned from the head into the tail: and the Gentiles from the tail into the head. Whence Moses in the book of Deuteronomy: *The stranger that sojourneth with thee shall go up above thee: he shall be for the head, and thou shalt be for the tail.* But yet neither all the first nor all the last belong to the number of the elect.

notes.text: It — The divine forbearance sparing Nineveh.
Was not this — Did I not think of this? That thy pardon would contradict my preaching.
Than to live — Disgraced and upbraided by hardened sinners, who will brand me for a liar.
A booth — Some small and mean shed, probably of green boughs. 'Till he might see - It seems the forty days were not fully expired.

Prepared — Commanded that in the place where Jonah's booth stood, this spreading plant should spring up to be a shade when the gathered boughs were withered. To deliver - To give some ease to his mind.
Prepared — By the same power which caused the gourd suddenly to spring, and spread itself. It smote - Which early next morning, bit the root, so that the whole gourd withered.

A east wind — A dry, scorching, blasting wind. Fainted - Overcome by the heat. Better to die - But Jonah must be wiser, and humbler, and more merciful too, e'er he die. Before God hath done with him, he will teach him to value his own life more, and to be more tender of the life of others.
I do well to be angry — If in the violence of this passion I should die (as some have) yet were I not to blame. What a speech! Verily the law made nothing perfect!
laboured — Thou didst not set it. Grow - Nor didst thou water or give growth to it.

I — The God of infinite compassions and goodness. That great city - Wouldest thou have me less merciful to such a goodly city, than thou art to a weed? Who cannot discern - Here are more than six-score innocents who are infants. Much cattle - Beside men, women and children who are in Nineveh, there are many other of my creatures that are not sinful, and my tender mercies are and shall be over all my works. If thou wouldest be their butcher, yet I will be their God. Go Jonah, rest thyself content and be thankful: that goodness, which spared Nineveh, hath spared thee in this thy inexcusable frowardness. I will be to repenting Nineveh what I am to thee, a God gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and I will turn from the evil which thou and they deserve.

glossa.text:
*Praise, for David himself.* ((CAS.)) This psalm contains briefly the things which in the divine Scriptures are spread abroad at large, etc., *as far as* lest any should be able to err in his praise:

((AUG.)) God fills the saints with the Holy Spirit, etc., *as far as* and therefore let his spirit in his servants praise him, because he makes himself to be praised.

((CAS.)) As there are seven psalms of penance, so also seven spirits, according to that sacrament wherein the Lord commanded Moses to set seven lamps in the tabernacle, shining with perpetual light.

*I will extol thee.* ((CAS.)) First the prophet promises endless praise; secondly, he says that all shall accomplish the praise of God in nine ways, there, *Generation and generation;* thirdly, he explains the same at greater length, there, *compassionate.*

*For ever and ever.* ((CAS.)) He who does not begin here shall be dumb in the world to come.

*Every day,* etc. ((ID.)) He who here every day does so, shall deserve in the eternal day to praise with continual exultation.

 ((AUG.)) He blesses now *every day,* that, when the one day without ends *fines*; read *fine*, "without end" shall have come, he may go from praise to praise, as from virtue to virtue. *For ever, and for ever and ever.* ((CAS.)) Of which praise elsewhere: *They shall praise for ever and ever ((Psal. XXXVIII))*, because they will always love him whom they will always see, since nothing is more delightful than that vision.
*Exceedingly.* ((CAS.)) In one word he has given us to consider that which cannot be fully grasped: and therefore never cease from praises.

*Generation and generation.* ((CAS.)) Secondly, he promises that all shall accomplish the praise of God in nine ways. *Thy works.* ((AUG.)) If we fail in his greatness, let us at least praise the worker from his works, the founder from the things founded, the creator from his creatures. ((CAS.)) Nine are the works: power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, strength, the greatness of terrible things, memory, justice, which shall be explained hereafter: from these, as from topics and seeds, all praise is drawn, in the manner in which all arguments are taken from a small number of topics. *And thy power.* ((AUG.)) For works do not praise, save that they may announce the strength of the worker. But certain eloquent men praise the creature, forgetful of the Creator. But holy praisers, if they love the works, praise the worker the more: and on account of these they love him. If in things made there is felt any beauty, usefulness, strength, it is the more praised in him who made it. If thou praisest the works, thou praisest thyself also, who art the work of God. And this occurs: *Let not thy own mouth praise thee, lest thou seem arrogant ((Prov. XXVII))*. But it is not arrogance, because thou praisest God in thee, not thyself.

*And the power.* If he did not threaten, there would be no correction *corectio*; but if he did not allure, there would be no exhortation. He is therefore both lovable and terrible. They shall declare therefore the power of him that disciplines and punishes, if they preach the eternal kingdom, they do not keep silent concerning the eternal fire.

*They shall belch forth the memory of the abundance of thy sweetness.* ((AUG.)) He himself through his abundant sweetness is first mindful of us, by calling us, by preventing us with his grace, and thence we of him.

*They shall belch forth,* he says, not, they shall eat.

((AUG.)) He eats who learns, he belches forth who teaches: yet he belches forth that which he eats. This memory, because it is exceeding sweet, is to be eaten and to be belched forth. So then eat, that thou mayest belch forth.

*Compassionate and merciful.* ((CAS.)) Thirdly he explains at greater length the things which in the second place he set forth briefly. As if: Deservedly in these things they shall praise, because *compassionate,* etc. The parts of praise are set down here which were set down above, but they cannot be explained one by one: for who could fully explain his works or his power? ((AUG.)) *Compassionate and merciful.* To those to whom he has given that pardon. *Patient.* To those to whom he has not yet given it, but waits that he may give it.

notes.text: To me to live is Christ — To know, to love, to follow Christ, is my life, my glory, my joy.

Here he begins to treat of the former clause of the preceding verse. Of the latter he treats, chap. ii, 17. But if I am to live is the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour — This is the fruit of my living longer, that I can labour more. Glorious labour! desirable fruit! in this view, long life is indeed a blessing. And what I should choose I know not - That is, if it were left to my choice.
To depart — Out of bonds, flesh, the world. And to be with Christ - In a nearer and fuller union. It is better to depart; it is far better to be with Christ.
I know — By a prophetic notice given him while he was writing this. That I shall continue some time longer with you - And doubtless he did see them after this confinement.

Only — Be careful for this, and nothing else. Stand fast in one spirit - With the most perfect unanimity. Striving together - With united strength and endeavours. For the faith of the gospel - For all the blessings revealed and promised therein.
Which — Namely, their being adversaries to the word of God, and to you the messengers of God. Is an evident token - That they are in the high road to perdition; and you, in the way of salvation.
For to you it is given — As a special token of God's love, and of your being in the way of salvation.
Having the same kind of conflict with your adversaries, which ye saw in me — When I was with you, Acts xvi, 12, 19, &c.

glossa.text: *But to me to live is Christ,* etc. As if he would say: Deservedly do I magnify Christ, whether by life or by death, because *Christ is to me to live,* that is, he is life to me here through faith and hope, and in the future through sight. For this life he delivered up his mortal body, that he may receive that same body immortal for ever, whence he also subjoins, and to die is gain.

*But if to live,* etc. Christ is to me to live, that I may magnify him. And if that is so, then I know not which I should choose, to die or to live. As if: Unless this fruit were, there would be no doubt but that I would choose to die, that I might have Christ for my reward: and therefore, do not doubt to die for Christ.
*But to abide,* etc. Behold, he chooses not what is better for himself, but what is expedient for many, on account of charity, which is to be chosen before all things.
*And the joy of faith,* etc. That is: That we may rejoice over your faith, or that you may rejoice over the faith, advancing in it. Which is not save where there is a clean conscience.
*And this from God,* etc. Even that which you suffer is not from you, but from God: because, for the merit of Christ who obeyed the Father, this among the other graces has been given to you.
*Not only,* etc. Both therefore pertain to the grace of God, both the faith of them that believe and the endurance of them that suffer, because he said that both were given.
*Such as you have both seen in me.* When I was scourged naked on account of the pythoness woman out of whom I shut out the malignant spirit, who furnished great gain to her masters.

notes.text: That some of those who were first called may yet be last, our Lord confirms by the following parable: of which the primary scope is, to show, That many of the Jews would be rejected, and many of the Gentiles accepted; the secondary, That of the Gentiles, many who were first converted would be last and lowest in the kingdom of glory; and many of those who were last converted would be first, and highest therein. The kingdom of heaven is like — That is, the manner of God's proceeding in his kingdom resembles that of a householder. In the morning - At six, called by the Roman and Jews, the first hour. From thence reckoning on to the evening, they called nine, the third hour; twelve, the sixth; three in the afternoon, the ninth; and five, the eleventh. To hire labourers into his vineyard - All who profess to be Christians are in this sense labourers, and are supposed during their life to be working in God's vineyard.
The Roman penny was about seven pence halfpenny. [About thirteen and three quarter cents, American.] This was then the usual price of a day's labour.
About the eleventh hour — That is, very late; long after the rest were called.
In the evening — Of life; or of the world.

Who were hired about the eleventh hour — Either the Gentiles, who were called long after the Jews into the vineyard of the Church of Christ; or those in every age who did not hear, or at least understand the Gospel call, till their day of life was drawing to a period. Some circumstances of the parable seem best to suit the former, some the latter of these senses.
The first supposed they should have received more — Probably the first here may mean the Jews, who supposed they should always be preferred before the Gentiles.

Thou hast made them equal to us — So St. Peter expressly, Acts xv, 9. God-hath put no difference between us (Jews) and them, (Gentiles, ) purifying their hearts by faith. And those who were equally holy here, whenever they were called, will be equally happy hereafter.

It is my will to give to this last called among the heathens even as to the first called among the Jews: yea, and to the late converted publicans and sinners, even as to those who, were called long before.

Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? — Yea, doubtless, to give either to Jew or Gentile a reward infinitely greater than he deserves. But can it be inferred from hence, that it is lawful, or possible, for the merciful Father of spirits to "Consign an unborn soul to hell? Or damn him from his mother's womb?" Is thine eye evil because I am good - Art thou envious, because I am gracious? Here is an evident reference to that malignant aspect, which is generally the attendant of a selfish and envious temper.

So the last shall be first, and the first last — Not only with regard to the Jews and Gentiles, but in a thousand other instances. For many are called - All who hear the Gospel; but few chosen - Only those who obey it. Matt. xix, 30; xxii, 14.

glossa.text: *The kingdom is like.* He shows by a parable that the first shall be last, and the last first. This father of the household is our Creator, who has a vineyard, the universal Church, which from Abel to the last of the elect who is to be born at the end has sent forth as many branches as it has brought forth saints. This father went out to dress his vineyard in the morning, at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, the eleventh he hired workmen, from the beginning of this world to its end: he does not cease to send preachers to school the people of the faithful. *The kingdom is like.* Not to the man only, but to the whole business carried on by the man, and so likewise in like cases. *Early in the morning.* Plainly he began from the first just man to invite preachers, with an everlasting wage, to plant the Church.

*By agreement.* That is, by a confirmed promise that they should be reformed to the image of God, if by building up the Church they should press on in the commandments of the decalogue.

*For a penny. ((HIER.))* The penny bears the image of the king, etc., *as far as* or in your last days come to your senses.

*From the last even unto,* etc. Because those who at the Lord's coming have been called to the kingdom arrive without any lateness, equal to those who began from the beginning of the world, all indeed have the same heaven, but star differs from star in brightness. He began from the last, when he brought the thief into paradise before Peter. Because those who come late are sometimes rewarded first, because they go forth out of the body before those who were called in boyhood.

*Or is it not lawful.* A foolish question against the goodness of God. The thing to be asked would be, not whether he gave what he did not owe: but whether he did not give what he did owe. *Is thy eye,* etc. Truly the Jews had a crooked intent, who forbade the apostles to speak to the Gentiles, that they might be saved.

*So the last shall be first. ((AUG.))* That is, the Jews shall be turned from the head into the tail: and the Gentiles from the tail into the head. Whence Moses in the book of Deuteronomy: *The stranger that sojourneth with thee shall go up above thee: he shall be for the head, and thou shalt be for the tail.* But yet neither all the first nor all the last belong to the number of the elect.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The landowner went out at dawn, and at noon, and at the eleventh hour.
The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all.
Are you envious because I am generous?
The Lord is gracious and slow to anger.
We who came late are paid in full.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.
Come, let us worship the God whose grace offends our arithmetic.
We come to the generous God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Stand in the marketplace as the long day ends, the light going gold, certain you have been passed over — and hear the voice that says, you also, come.
The Lord is gracious and good to all.
We keep our ledgers of who worked longest and who deserves the most.
The Lord is gracious and good to all.
But God opens his hand to the latecomer, the outsider, even to Nineveh, even to us.
The Lord is gracious and good to all.
The first will be last and the last first, and the wage is the same: grace.
The Lord is gracious and good to all.
So come, whatever the hour, and receive what you could not earn.
The Lord is gracious and good to all. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: At the eleventh hour the call still comes: you also, come.
God is good to all.
We count who deserves the most.
God is good to all.
But grace is not a wage; it is a gift.
God is good to all.
Come, whatever the hour, and worship.
We come to the generous God. Amen.

turn.gravity: The day pairs Jonah — furious on his hill that God spared Nineveh — with the Psalm's slow-to-anger mercy and the vineyard's equal denarius. One nerve runs through all three: God's generosity offends the deserving. Grace is not fair, and the longest-serving resent it most.
turn.trap: It becomes a lesson about fairness (and how the workers should have read the fine print), or a warm word that "God rewards everyone" — either way the scandal is explained off. The parable's offense is precisely the equal wage; defuse it and there is no sermon left.
turn.hinge: The householder does no one wrong — every promise is kept — and the first are still furious. Grace that is genuinely unfair to our accounting. The only question the text leaves open is whether you can rejoice in that or only resent it.

doors.claim: The wage is eternal life itself, and it is given whole to everyone — heaven is not a pay scale, and the latecomer is not shortchanged.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: The denarius here I take to mean salvation itself.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Because life eternal shall be equal to all the saints, one denarius is given to all — though in that life the light of merits will still shine diversely.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The denarius bears the figure of the King: you have received my image and likeness. What more do you desire?

doors.say: What you are paid is God's own life, given to you entire — there is no larger wage to envy.
doors.do: Lead them to receive the denarius as gift, not earnings — to name where they have been counting their hours instead of marvelling at the coin.

doors.claim: The hours are the ages of the world; the last hired are the latecomers — the Gentiles, the deathbed convert, anyone called after us — and they are seated as our equals.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: The morning is the age from Adam to Noah, the third hour Noah to Abraham, the sixth and ninth to Moses and to the Lord, and the eleventh hour from the Lord's coming to the end of the world.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The eleventh hour: the Gentiles, called long after the Jews into the vineyard of the Church — or those in any age who were called late.

doors.say: You may have worked since morning, but the kingdom is not seniority — the one called at the eleventh hour sits beside you, equal.
doors.do: Turn long-time members from a claim of priority to gladness at the latecomer — one person they would secretly rank below themselves.

doors.claim: The laborers were not cheated of anything; their grievance is simply that others got more than they deserved — and that envy of grace is the sin the parable exposes in us.

witnesses.author: Remigius of Auxerre
witnesses.reading: By the eye is meant the purpose: they had an evil eye, an evil purpose, because they were grieved at the salvation of the others.

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Their complaint was not that they were defrauded of their wage, but that the others received more than they deserved — for the envious have as much pain at another's good as at their own ill.

doors.say: Search the resentment in your own chest when grace runs to someone who didn't earn it — that evil eye, not the wage, is the danger here.
doors.do: Send them, like Jonah left outside the city, to one place they are angry that God has been merciful, and to repent of the grudge.

synthesis.convergence: Jonah sulks that grace reached his enemies; the Psalm praises a God who is good to all and slow to anger; Paul counts his own advantage as nothing next to Christ and others; and the laborers seethe at an equal wage. Together they press one nerve: God's generosity offends the deserving.
synthesis.claim: Grace is not fair — and that is the best news in the world, unless you have been keeping count of your hours.
synthesis.here: For long-faithful church people — the first-hired, the elder brothers, the Jonahs — the move is to catch the resentment in their own chest when grace runs to the latecomer, and to let God's gentle 'are you angry?' turn them from the gate back to the feast.

turn.subtract: Three doors, three landings — wonder at the equal coin, humility before the latecomer, repentance of the evil eye. They cannot all be preached at once; pick the one your people most need and let the other two go.
